evaluation.positioning_hook: An FBI surveillance agent chasing missing ex-cons in Silver Lake stumbles into a comet-fueled conspiracy, a hidden basement dungeon, and the possibility that her own childhood disappearance was never what she believed.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise has a clean commercial engine: an FBI sting, a creepy suburban house, and a bigger conspiracy tied to a comet. The audience is narrower than a four-quadrant thriller because the script leans hard into paranoia, grief, and a late-stage reality shift, but the hook is strong and easy to sell.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands early with Rico tailing the orange pickup and discovering the red-door/blue-door split, then deepens fast with the hidden hatch, foil-lined rooms, and comet obsession. The premise is easy to explain in two sentences and keeps mutating in a way that stays legible.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Rico is a strong lead because her competence, insecurity, and buried family wound all drive the case. Cole is a vivid partner with real personality, and Watson/James/Henry each add texture, though the script is still most durable around Rico’s POV rather than a broad ensemble.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script takes a familiar surveillance-thriller setup and pushes it into occult-conspiracy/body-horror territory without losing the procedural spine. The foil, bell, comet, and sound-based control system give it a distinct identity rather than a generic mystery wrapper.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The first half is built on escalating discoveries, then the back half keeps turning the screw with the support group, the second house, the dungeon reveal, and the Watson betrayal. The story keeps generating new questions and reversals, with very little dead air once the stakeout begins.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The script’s core idea is immediately graspable but still strange: a surveillance case about missing ex-cons turns into a hidden system of predation managed by the FBI. The comet mythology and Rico’s false-memory childhood wound make the reveal feel both surprising and inevitable.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The LA neighborhoods, FBI bullpen, surveillance van, support group, and suburban duplex create a specific social world with useful texture. The world becomes especially story-generating once the foil-lined underground system and the bureau’s quiet complicity are introduced.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script has a very specific paranoid register: procedural banter, deadpan workplace friction, and escalating cosmic dread all live in the same lane. The sound design motifs, the bell, the chewing, and the comet imagery give it a hard-to-mistake tonal signature.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: The story suggests a larger mythology around the comet, the disappearances, and Rico’s childhood memory, but it still plays primarily as a contained feature mystery. There’s enough buried material to feel bigger than the plot on the page, though the script is not withholding at a Severance-level.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Rico/Cole is a strong engine, and Watson/James/Henry each create meaningful pressure on that dynamic. The relationships are not just functional; they generate conflict, misdirection, and emotional payoff, even if the script is still structurally anchored to one lead.

lead_characters.name: Lucia Del Rico
lead_characters.demographics: Woman, early 30s, FBI agent; Latina; emotionally guarded, work-obsessed, carrying unresolved childhood trauma.
lead_characters.hook: A sharp, hyper-vigilant FBI surveillance agent who wants to be taken seriously and trusted on instinct, but whose buried grief makes her vulnerable to pattern-making and obsession. She’s competent in the field, socially prickly, and increasingly convinced that the missing-ex-con case is tied to the night her mother vanished; the script keeps testing whether her intuition is insight or self-deception.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Jodie Foster in The Silence of the Lambs or Amy Adams in Sharp Objects: a controlled, inward performance that has to carry procedural authority, emotional fracture, and a late-breaking identity crisis. It gives an actor a full-spectrum role—deadpan command, panic, grief, and final defiance.

lead_characters.name: Dale Cole
lead_characters.demographics: Man, 60s, FBI agent; older, world-weary, nearing retirement.
lead_characters.hook: A veteran surveillance agent with a filthy sense of humor, a tired body, and a surprising amount of emotional intelligence. He starts as comic friction and ends as the script’s most human institutional voice, the guy who knows the job has cost him a marriage and still believes in doing it right.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor do what Bryan Cranston did in Breaking Bad’s quieter stretches or what JK Simmons did in Whiplash: authority, weariness, and a late emotional reveal without losing the character’s bite. It’s a scene-stealing supporting part with real warmth and bite.

lead_characters.name: Captain Watson
lead_characters.demographics: Man, 50s, FBI station chief; polished, commanding, institutionally powerful.
lead_characters.hook: A smooth, paternal bureau boss who reads as pragmatic until the script reveals he’s the architect of the entire hidden system. He weaponizes reassurance, bureaucracy, and institutional language, making him the story’s most chilling authority figure because he never stops sounding reasonable.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the controlled menace of Bryan Cox in Succession or Michael Shannon in Boardwalk Empire: calm, articulate power that turns predatory. The showcase is in playing the smile that never reaches the threat underneath.

lead_characters.name: Henry Dodson
lead_characters.demographics: Man, middle-aged, ex-convict; physically ordinary, increasingly unstable, later revealed as part of the system.
lead_characters.hook: At first he reads like the suspect in a missing-persons case, then becomes a frightened intermediary trying to warn Rico without being able to say the whole truth. He’s creepy, pathetic, and oddly sympathetic, which makes his eventual role in the larger machine more unsettling.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor do what Paul Dano did in Prisoners or what Ben Mendelsohn does so well in crime stories: ordinary surface, deep unease, and a slow reveal of hidden desperation. The big play is the transformation from suspect to terrified participant.

lead_characters.name: James White
lead_characters.demographics: Man, 30s, ex-convict and support-group attendee; emotionally open, lonely, vulnerable.
lead_characters.hook: A grieving son who seems like a possible ally and romantic connection before the script reveals he’s another piece of the machinery. He’s the most emotionally accessible of the supporting players, which makes his turn into a compromised asset land harder.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the intimacy and volatility of Jesse Plemons in a pressure-cooker drama: tender, wounded, and then terrifyingly pliable. It’s a strong showcase for playing sincerity that curdles.

lead_characters.name: Hope
lead_characters.demographics: Woman, 30s-40s, suburban homeowner; controlled, eerie, physically precise.
lead_characters.hook: At first she seems like a strange prepper with a comet fixation, but she becomes one of the story’s most unnerving embodiments of the hidden system. She’s calm, ritualized, and frighteningly committed to the logic of the house.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the unnerving stillness of Toni Collette in Hereditary or Rebecca Hall in The Night House: domestic surface, existential dread underneath. The showcase is in making ordinary behavior feel ritualistic and wrong.

lead_characters.name: Lear
lead_characters.demographics: Man, 30s-40s, suburban homeowner; polished, deferential, increasingly monstrous.
lead_characters.hook: Hope’s partner and the story’s most unsettling domestic enabler, he performs normalcy while helping maintain the hidden basement system. He’s the kind of character whose politeness becomes more disturbing the more you understand him.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a great role for an actor who can play charm as camouflage, like Matthew Rhys in The Americans or Michael C. Hall in Dexter. The fun is in letting the audience realize too late how much control he actually has.

casting_characteristics: Lead role requires a strong emotional close-up performer who can carry procedural authority and paranoia
Supporting cast skews 30s-60s with one older male authority role

notable_requirements: FBI field office and surveillance van
two adjacent suburban houses with a shared garage and basement access

technical.vfx_details: Primarily comet enhancement, atmospheric sky work, and a few subjective light/flash effects; no heavy creature or digital-environment dependence.
technical.sfx_needs: Practical blood, concussion makeup, foil-wrapped body effects, dog bite gag, and a few controlled fight/tackle beats.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release; best positioned as a streamer original or specialty theatrical genre title

budget.note: Contemporary and mostly contained, but the night-heavy LA shoot, multiple house interiors, surveillance setups, practical blood work, and animal work keep this above a lean indie floor.

casting.note: The lead needs an actor who can play procedural competence, paranoia, and emotional fracture in the same frame, while Watson and Cole both need strong, specific performers to keep the institutional dynamic alive.

development.note: The script’s final reveal reframes the entire case as a hidden predation system tied to the comet and Watson, so the buyer is really evaluating a conspiracy-thriller mythology as much as a procedural mystery.

comp_set.title: The Invitation
comp_set.why_it_comps: Like this script, it turns a domestic setting into a paranoia machine and keeps the audience locked into a character’s increasingly unreliable read on the room.

comp_set.title: Prisoners
comp_set.why_it_comps: The missing-persons engine, suburban dread, and moral rot beneath a seemingly ordinary investigation are the same commercial lane.

comp_set.title: The Vast of Night
comp_set.why_it_comps: The comet/sky mystery and the sense of a larger unseen system give it the same eerie, low-key cosmic unease.

comp_set.title: The Night House
comp_set.why_it_comps: A grief-driven lead, a haunted domestic space, and a slow reveal that the protagonist’s memory is part of the mystery.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adults who like elevated genre thrillers with a strong female lead, a conspiracy hook, and a creepy domestic reveal.
audience_target.demographics: 25-54, slightly female-skewing but playable male; urban/suburban genre audience; strong appeal to viewers who like prestige thrillers and mystery-horror hybrids.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary locations, limited cast, practical effects, and a mostly contained LA-night shoot keep this in indie feature territory despite the high-concept reveal.

lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the lane where character psychology, mystery architecture, and a strong central performance matter as much as the genre turn. The script has enough hook for a buyer looking for a smart, creepy, adult thriller without requiring tentpole scale.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature. The world is suggestive, but there is no clean spinoff vector beyond this story’s central Rico/Watson/comet conspiracy.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The red-door/blue-door setup is instantly ownable.
strengths.what_it_means: That visual rule gives the movie a clean marketing image and a memorable audience puzzle from the first act. Buyers can sell the premise in one breath because the house geometry becomes the mystery engine.
strengths.evidence: The stakeout lands on two identical houses with only red and blue doors, and the script turns that choice into the central investigative problem.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Rico is a real lead role, not just a plot function.
strengths.what_it_means: The script gives a buyer a performance-driven package anchor: a female lead with authority, vulnerability, and a buried wound that pays off in the third act. That’s exactly the kind of role that can attract a serious actor and elevate the whole project.
strengths.evidence: Her first-case nerves, her friction with Cole, and the mother-disappearance flashbacks all feed the same emotional engine.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The procedural spine keeps the weirdness grounded.
strengths.what_it_means: The FBI surveillance mechanics, warrant pressure, and stakeout tactics make the movie feel playable and credible even as it escalates into conspiracy horror. That balance broadens the buyer pool because the script never abandons the crime-thriller lane entirely.
strengths.evidence: The van surveillance, bug placement, probable-cause debate, and SWAT coordination all play as concrete procedural beats.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The comet mythology gives the thriller a bigger shadow.
strengths.what_it_means: The cosmic element adds scale without requiring expensive spectacle, which is a strong commercial move for an indie feature. It also gives the movie a hook that feels larger than the house plot and helps it stand out in a crowded thriller market.
strengths.evidence: Comet Theora is repeatedly referenced, tracked on forums, and tied to the disappearances and Rico’s childhood memory.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Cole is a scene-stealing partner with emotional payoff.
strengths.what_it_means: The lead-partner dynamic gives the script a second selling point beyond the mystery: a veteran mentor who is funny, human, and ultimately tragic. That kind of role helps with casting and gives the movie a stronger emotional landing.
strengths.evidence: His banter, retirement jokes, marriage confession, and final sacrifice all deepen the relationship.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The hidden-system reveal is a strong genre escalation.
strengths.what_it_means: The movie doesn’t just reveal a killer; it reveals an institutional machine, which makes the ending feel bigger and more unsettling. That kind of escalation is attractive to buyers because it turns a contained mystery into a conspiracy thriller with teeth.
strengths.evidence: Watson’s dungeon, the foil-lined rooms, the creatures, and the bureau’s complicity all reframe the case.

whats_special.headline: This is a contained, elevated thriller with a memorable visual hook, a strong female lead, and a conspiracy reveal that expands the movie without blowing up the budget. It has the kind of clear market image and performance opportunity that can get a buyer to lean in fast, especially in the streamer/specialty genre lane.

items.area: The final mythology is a big swing.
items.detail: The script pivots from procedural surveillance thriller into comet-linked body-horror conspiracy, and that’s the sharpest buyer conversation on the page. It’s a bold escalation, but it also means the movie is asking the audience to accept a major reality shift after spending a long stretch in grounded FBI mode.

items.area: Watson’s turn is doing a lot of work.
items.detail: The captain moves from paternal boss to hidden architect of the system, and the reveal depends on the audience buying that institutional mask for most of the movie. That’s a strong twist, but it narrows the casting and performance lane because the role has to stay credible while hiding the true engine.

items.area: The comet thread is intriguing but abstract.
items.detail: Comet Theora is a compelling motif, but for much of the script it functions more as atmosphere than as a concrete causal force. Buyers will weigh whether the mythology feels sufficiently specific before the late reveal, or whether it reads as a stylish overlay on the real story.

items.area: The ending depends on a very specific tonal balance.
items.detail: The final movement has to hold procedural aftermath, grief, cosmic dread, and a last-image sting in the Bora Bora coda. That’s a lot of tonal territory to land in one feature, and the script’s commercial ceiling will be judged partly on whether that blend feels controlled rather than overstuffed.

issues.headline: The script’s biggest friction is also its biggest ambition: it starts as a clean FBI surveillance thriller and then asks the buyer to follow it into a much stranger conspiracy-horror register. If that pivot lands, it’s a real differentiator; if it doesn’t, the movie risks feeling like two strong ideas stitched together.
